questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My studies are Korean studies, so being in Korea seems a given. And EWHA has a good reputation in Korea, so wanted to experience it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Given that I've been to Korea before it was fairly easy. As for the messages from EWHA, I only look through those regarding arriving fast, but from what I could see they were fairly helpful.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None, seeing I've been there before and already know.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: If you've never been I recommend the 'Peace Buddy Program' Ewha offers. It's a Korean student of EWHA, and they're very helpful with anything you should need.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Airbnb (remember to check with the host that they'll be able to provide the documentations you'll need from them later when applying for the FRC (mandatory residence permit you'll need to apply for. The university will inform you about this in due time))

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It's more expensive. I preferred it because I just don't do well with sharing a room with someone. I need to be able to close a door and be myself.
But the dorm on ehwa is super cheap, covers all the bills in the rent, and I heard from others they were happy with it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Check out the courses offered ahead of time and make a list with the class courses so you're ready!!!, and make sure you have super fast internet (using a PC café is recommended and cheap), the courses is filled up soooo fast!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You do it only on ehwa's portal (school will inform you how to when it nears). Check out the website in general some days ahead, so you can navigate the page, because it is a little confusing. I had my address and Korean phone number ready in an open word so I could just copy paste, because they ask you to fill these things out before you choose courses. When that is done there is an area where you write in the course code (XXXXX-XX). And then you just press the save button (or called something like that, can't remember exactly). If you're accepted to the course, it will simply appear on the list. If there is no room a small information box will appear. And then you keep going like that till you have all the course credits you need.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The school provides you a written guide how to, with pictures too. But actually sitting and doing it, you're on your own.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all of them (PC café).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Listed in the box 'Please describe the registration process at your host institution'.
Also, PC café.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It really depends on the professor. Some classes where challenging and wonderful, and others felt like high-school (gymnasium) level. As well as some made you use your tools and think for yourself, while other professor just want you to remember what they said, and repeat that back.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It's hard to compare when it's two very different cultures and approaches to studying.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Sex, Gender, Sexuality in Korea (835743-01), Current Issues (10596-01), Social Problems in Contemporary Global World (10905-01), K-MOOC: Identity, Agency, Equality, and Security in the Age of AI (11372-01) & Contemporary Photography (11164-01)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Current Issues and K-MOOC - it's the same professor and she's wonderful and one of the professors that makes you think and not just repeat back. Contemporary Photography was wonderful as well, as it helped me see new perspective to - and history of photography.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
It's always shocking how much I spend on food and experiences xD
They're not expensive, I just do a lot so it adds up.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Fruit is ridiculously expensive and duvet + pillows.
But generally for food, use their online shopping 'coupang' if you can (amazing!), if not go for the super market E-mart and shop their label 'No brand'.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Offered only a little and stupid expensive.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a Chuseok celebration, Sports day and ending semester day. as well as some field trips.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Well, of course go for all if you want to and for the company, you should :) But otherwise I recommend you do the 'field trips' on your own, if you can manage, as it won't be as expensive then.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Oh my gosh - so much! Budget: subway/train travel to different parts of Seoul or even out of. There are free offers, or very cheap experiences (especially all of their cafés, so pretty!) but parts of the city as well have mural cities, statues, palaces (their entrance is cheap but free on chuseok, so on...
Klook, Trip, and Creatrip are apps offers to foreigners in Korea, and have good deals. I especially recommend Klook's cooking courses or DMZ tour (which is otherwise so must of a hassle to figure out on your own).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy as I've been there before.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
It's hard. Either they're f bois, want very superficial friendships with foreigners because that's trending, or they're extremely sweet and genuine people but shy because they might not be to comfortable with foreign culture or confident in English.
It was easier for me because I speak Korean.
But try the peace buddy program, speak with those in your classes (as they usually will know enough English) and then usually they'll further introduce you to their friend group.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not challenging, but just be aware; no talking on public transportation (considered really rude), they spit everywhere on the street (all ages and sexes), you will get starred at (not in a bad way at all, they're just very curious about you, but it can feel overwhelming at times), give and receive with two hands (sign of respect), respect personal sphere! (seriously don't hug, unless you know them well and know they're okay with it), remember to slightly bow when greeting, saying thank you or sorry. I think with those you're prepared for most.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I've gotten help or offered help from many elders. If you know a few words or cultural things they'll be so happy. So many side dishes when you just ordered one thing. The food!!! The convenience stores are open 24/7, good and cheap. Public transportation works so good and fast (just avoid rush hour (roughly 7-9 am & 5-7 pm), if you can, it's awful!!). Beautiful cultural/historical sites everywhere. Just love, love, love!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Learn very basic words - like hello, thank you and sorry.
2. Uni's buddy programme!
3. Socialize with other exchange students, if the Koreans in your classes are hard to get close to - just don't be all alone and have no one you can call.
(4. phone numbers: 1345 - is for immigration help center, 1330 - Korea travel hotline, general information, translation service, police etc. provided in English) (
https://10mag.com/free-resources-for-foreigners-in-korea/
)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I really varies with information shared by EWHA. Sometimes they're great and sometimes you have to find it yourself. Especially finding your way around campus can be a bit confusing at first. Seriously - peace buddy program! sign up :)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All of it. Of coursed I'm biased, being a Korean Studies student, but I absolutely loved it all.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being alone. You're so far away from home. Find friends. Buddy program, people in class, other exchange students, Facebook groups (especially recommend 'expat women living in korea' (can't remember exact wording)) - just don't be alone, have at least one person.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
I recommend Chingu mobile for Korean phone number and it's cheaper if you buy from home and set it to 'pick up'.
Respect personal sphere as much as possible (no hugging people), give and take with two hands (especially with money), no talking on public transportation, free wifi basically everywhere, common to leave your stuff on tables, chairs, picnic blankets and no one will take it, get a T-money transportation card (in airport before entrance to train or convenience stores), easy to refill on subway stations or convenience stores, get 'papago' (app)!!!, absolut best translator for Korean (writing, live audio transaction, pictures...), Naver (app)!!! (google maps don't work in korea, naver is the Koreans own ''google maps''), Kakao T app (just need a Korean phone number and Kakao chat to set up, and then you can see the prices as you book a cab, choose 'pay to driver', and they can't cheat you price wise), Kakao (their texting app, little like messenger, you cannot avoid having to use it), conversion is roughly 'delete two zeroes and then half' - so 20.000 won, roughly 100 dkk, 2.500 won roughly 12,5 dkk. Cheapest bank to withdraw money - those on campus or KB ATMS (always 3.500 won). Dress however you want, of course, just know that in Korean culture, short skirt (even very, very short) is high fashion, but cleavage, collarbones, shoulders and such is a big no go. 

Not to scare you (honestly, Korea is very safe!!), but just watch out for the f bois (saying things like: 'are you russian'? = [if you're up for a one-night stand], are you open-minded? = one night stand, do you live alone? = availability for a room for s*x and so on....) and cults. It's especially if someone starts talking to you out of nowhere in the public (and especially Hongdae, Sinchon and Myeongdong), because it is so NOT in their culture to do that. It really doesn't happen too often (I hope I'm not scaring you), but just be aware and walk away when it does, especially with the cults (they'll usually start talking about god, or ancestors and such and maybe offer tea in a café nearby - just leave immediately). Also, Sindorim (신도림
/신도림동) is not a place you want to be, especially as a solo woman.
Watch out for hidden cameras - people taking your picture (especially up skirts, is unfortunately happening a lot) and if you spot any holes in toilet stalls.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
